slides.headline: This frog spends winter frozen, with no heartbeat.
slides.sub: Then it thaws in spring and carries on with life

slides.label: of its body water can turn to ice
slides.body: The ice forms outside the cells. Water is drawn out of them, so cells and organs shrink dramatically, but survive.

slides.headline: No heartbeat. No breathing.
slides.body: A frozen wood frog has no detectable vital signs: no heartbeat, breathing, blood circulation or brain activity. It stays that way for weeks or months.

slides.headline: Sugar as antifreeze
slides.body: As ice spreads, the liver makes huge amounts of glucose and sends it to every organ, where it stops cells losing too much water.
slides.source: Storey et al. (2021); Animal Diversity Web

slides.label: days frozen in a row, for wild wood frogs in Alaska
slides.body: Average winter lows were -14.6 °C, dipping to -18.1 °C. All 18 frogs tracked in their natural hibernation spots survived.
slides.source: Larson et al., J. Exp. Biol. (2014)

slides.headline: Frogs in the Arctic
slides.body: Its range runs from the southeastern US to the Brooks Range in Arctic Alaska, where it is the only amphibian found that far north.

slides.headline: Save this for the next cold snap.
slides.body: Survival stories, checked against the science. Follow @earthspirit_nature.

caption:
The wood frog (Lithobates sylvaticus) survives winter with most of its body water frozen, its heart and breathing stopped.

Freezing usually starts when ice touches the frog's skin, and it creeps slowly through the body over many hours. Wild frogs in Alaska carried 13 times more glucose in their muscles than frogs frozen in the lab, possibly built up by repeated freezing and thawing in early autumn.

Swipe for how a frog comes back from the ice. Sources on the last slide.
